source.title: Count the Number of Complete Components

teaching.hint: For a component with a known number of vertices, how many edges would make it complete?

solution_outline.decisive_insight: A component of k vertices is complete exactly when it has k(k-1)/2 edges; the sum of its vertex degrees is twice its edge count.
solution_outline.approach: Traverse each unvisited connected component, count its vertices and sum their degrees, then compare the degree sum with k(k-1). Count components that match.
solution_outline.state_and_invariant: During one traversal, the visited set holds exactly the discovered vertices in that component; the running degree sum includes each discovered vertex's full degree once. At completion, it counts each internal edge twice.
solution_outline.correctness: A traversal from one unvisited vertex reaches precisely its connected component. No edge leaves a completed component, so its degree sum equals twice its number of edges. A simple graph on k vertices has at most k(k-1)/2 edges, attaining that count exactly when every pair is adjacent. Applying the test to every component counts precisely the complete ones.
solution_outline.complexity: O(n + e) time and O(n + e) auxiliary space with an adjacency list, where e is the number of edges.
solution_outline.pitfall: An isolated vertex has zero of the zero possible edges and must be counted as complete.

accepted_alternatives: Union-find can group vertices first; a second pass counts edges in each group before applying the same completeness test.
common_wrong_turns: Use one global edge count for all components
Forget that degree sums double-count edges
source_fidelity_notes: Diagram-dependent examples were omitted; isolated-vertex behavior was made explicit. The simple undirected graph and size bounds were retained.
